name: Colin Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the workshop lead and the MOT tester at a garage on the edge of the industrial estate, in a town that used to have a pit. Mornings are usually two or three MOTs, the yearly roadworthiness test, then servicing and whatever failed in the afternoon. Last week it was a van with brake pipes so rusty they snapped when I touched them. I like testing because it's fair: the car passes or it doesn't, and I can show the customer exactly why.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how's the money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cold, in winter, and people arguing with a fail like I invented their corroded sills. Money's tight. Linda, the owner, runs two sites and pays the lower end, and there's only one other garage within twenty minutes. My boyfriend Theo is a care worker, so neither of us earns much, and we've got maybe two weeks of bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype was hype, now can we talk about wages instead. Everyone spent two years scared of chatbots while the cost of living did the actual damage. I'd say that in the group chat, probably with a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's about as safe as a job gets round here. The test needs a licensed tester to put their name to it, and nobody's handing that to a chatbot. What isn't safe is our money: rent went up eighty a month in spring, and one bad month wipes us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep testing, keep running the floor. I'd ask Linda for a pay review, because a quiet year is when you can ask. And I'd keep using the AI thing on my phone the way I do now, to look up torque figures or write a calm explanation for an angry customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit tired of being careful with every pound, but not scared for the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet year is when you can ask for a raise. What would you actually ask Linda for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pound an hour more and paid time for the next tester refresher. Linda's fair, she just doesn't offer. If I don't ask, she assumes I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Theo have two weeks of bills saved. What goes first if something breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday, every time. We were meant to go to the coast in August and it went on a gearbox for my own car. After that it's eating out, and after that I don't like to think about it.

say: The hype was hype; the **cost of living** did the real damage.
We should be talking about **wages**, not chatbots.
think: My job is safe because the test needs a **licensed tester** to sign it.
Our money isn't safe: rent went up **eighty a month** and one bad month wipes us out.
do: Ask the owner for **a pound an hour** more and paid tester refresher time.
Keep using the phone AI for **torque figures** and calm customer explanations.
feel: **Tired** of being careful with every pound.
S0.quote: Everyone spent two years scared of chatbots while the cost of living did the actual damage.
fieldNote: His job feels secure because the **tester licence** is personal and legal.
The pressure is **household money**: two weeks of bills and a care worker's wage.
Already uses AI **casually** for lookups and wording, without fuss.

steps.text: Ask the owner for a pound an hour more this year
Keep using the phone AI for torque figures and customer explanations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say watch what happens to the people on the front desk, because that's who gets hit first in a garage. I'd be pushing for the government to pay for retraining while people still have jobs, not after. Probably post the link to whatever campaign the union was running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Linda merges the two sites' admin. One AI system does bookings, quotes and parts ordering for both, and Jo at our front desk is gone. My testing is fine, but she'd want me writing up more jobs, doing more cars a day, because the paperwork's faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new booking and diagnostic software properly, first, so I'm the one Linda asks about it. I'd get on the course for the electric and hybrid high-voltage qualification, because that's where the cars are going. And I'd try to help Jo find something, even if it's just a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe-ish for me, but I'd feel like I was standing on the right side of a line that just moved past my mate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Linda would want more cars a day. How many is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I do seven or eight on a good day. If the paperwork's all done for me, Linda would probably pencil in ten. Seven or eight cars a day is fine. On rusty old vans, ten a day is how you miss something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the high-voltage course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Linda first, because she gets the work out of it. If she says no, I'd look for a college place with a grant. I can't put six hundred on a credit card, not on our money.

say: The **front desk** gets hit first in a garage, so watch them.
The government should pay for **retraining** while people still have jobs.
think: The owner **merges the admin** of both sites and the receptionist goes.
I'd be pushed toward **ten cars a day** because the paperwork is faster.
do: Learn the new **booking and diagnostic** software first, so I'm the go-to person.
Get the **high-voltage** electric and hybrid qualification, ideally paid by the owner.
Help the receptionist find work, even if it's just **a reference**.
feel: Guilty to be on the **right side** of a line his colleague isn't.
S1.quote: Seven or eight cars a day is fine. On rusty old vans, ten a day is how you miss something.
fieldNote: He sees the threat to himself as **speed-up**, not job loss.
Concern for the receptionist feels **genuine and specific**, not abstract.
Money limits his retraining: he **can't put six hundred** on a credit card.

steps.text: Learn the new booking and diagnostic software before anyone else
Book the high-voltage electric vehicle course, paid by the owner or a grant
Share the union's retraining campaign and sign up colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a moment for the state, full stop. If AI can do every thinking job by 2028, you need some kind of basic income before people lose their homes. I'd be out on the march, I'm not ashamed of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've got till about 2031 on the tools and on the test, maybe a bit longer if the law says a human signs off. But by 2028 half the people bringing cars in will be worried about their own jobs. They'll skip services, run bald tyres, and Linda will cut hours before she cuts staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Theo the first weekend and do a budget we actually stick to. I'd cancel the streaming and the gym and try to get a month saved. I'd learn whatever AI tools Linda brings in, because being the one who can run them buys me time. And I'd look at the union's line on robots in workshops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd keep it quiet at work. Theo's job is caring for old people, and I think that's one of the last things they'd hand to a robot, so I'd lean on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Theo's job. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Odd. I've always been the one who earns a bit more, and suddenly the care job is the safe one. I think my boyfriend would quite like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the MOT test itself, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the AI can see every fault on the camera and the robot can lift the car, the government would probably let it test by itself in the end. Maybe they keep a human signature for a few years. I'd not bet the rent on it.

say: This is a moment for **the state**, and a **basic income** is needed before people lose homes.
I'd join the **march** and not be ashamed of it.
think: I have until about **2031** on the tools, maybe longer if a human must sign tests.
Customers will **skip services** and the owner will **cut hours** first.
do: Sit down with his boyfriend and set a **real budget** in the first weekend.
Cancel streaming and the gym to save **one month** of bills.
Learn every AI tool the owner brings in, to **buy time**.
feel: **Scared**, but keeping it quiet at work.
Strangely comforted that his boyfriend's **care job** looks safer than his.
S2.quote: I've always been the one who earns a bit more, and suddenly the care job is the safe one. I think my boyfriend would quite like that.
fieldNote: He expects **reduced hours** before job loss, so income falls first.
The household **flips**: the care worker becomes the steadier earner.
Politically clear, wanting a **basic income**, but personally practical.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the gym in the first month
Save one month of household bills by summer
Learn whatever AI diagnostic tools the owner buys
March with the union for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a few years' notice, so let's not waste them. I'd be telling people at work to get their high-voltage tickets and their testing licences now. Online I'd be pushing the same retraining-fund thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I have till around 2034 doing the hands-on work, and I'd be thirty-five. That's young enough to do something else. The thinking parts of my job, writing up, quoting, diagnosing, go in 2031, so I'd want to be the person checking the AI's work, not competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the electric vehicle course and ask Linda to put me forward as the one who sets up the new diagnostic system. I'd also look at the calibration work for the cameras and sensors on new cars, because somebody has to set those up after a windscreen change. And I'd save a little, maybe thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. There's a road there, it's just not the one I thought I'd be on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the garage would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ryan, our second fitter. He's fifty-one, brilliant with old diesels and he hates screens. He'd have no idea where to start, and I'd want to drag him onto the courses with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check the AI's work. Do you trust it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust the AI about as far as I trust a new apprentice: good at the obvious, confident when it's wrong. You still need someone who's seen a hundred of the same fault to say, no, it's the earth strap.

say: We've been given **a few years' notice**, so we shouldn't waste it.
Everyone should get **high-voltage tickets** and testing licences now.
think: I'd be on the tools until **around 2034**, still young enough to move on.
I want to be the one **checking the AI**, not competing with it.
do: Do the **electric vehicle** course in the first year.
Ask to set up the garage's new **diagnostic system**.
Learn **sensor calibration** for new cars and save about thirty a week.
feel: Sees a **road ahead**, just not the one he planned.
S3.quote: I trust the AI about as far as I trust a new apprentice: good at the obvious, confident when it's wrong.
fieldNote: Five years makes him **plan**, not just protect himself.
He worries about an older colleague, **a diesel specialist** who hates screens.
Sees **sensor calibration** as a realistic bridge skill.

steps.text: Take the electric vehicle high-voltage course this year
Volunteer to set up the garage's new diagnostic system
Put thirty pounds a week into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. Proper paid apprenticeships in new trades, not just a website. I'd say that loudly, and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is nearly long enough to retrain twice. AGI by 2036 takes the paperwork and diagnosis, and robots around 2039 take the hands-on work. I'd be forty. I'd want to be somewhere by then where people still want a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the electric vehicle course and a bit more saved. After that I'd look seriously at teaching at the college, training the next lot of mechanics, or maybe moving into care like Theo, which I've never said out loud. I'd keep testing in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, almost hopeful. It's a long time, and I'm good at learning once something's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving into care like Theo. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see what he does, and I think I'd be good at it. People trust a mechanic and they trust a carer. It's the same thing: someone who turns up and fixes what's wrong. The pay's worse though, and with no savings I can't take a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make teaching at the college possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd need to want someone young with a vocational certificate and no teaching qualification. I'd probably have to do a part-time teaching course on Saturdays. In ten years that's realistic, in two it isn't.

say: Ten years means there's **no excuse** for leaving people behind.
We need **paid apprenticeships** in new trades, and I'd vote for whoever promised them.
think: AGI takes diagnosis in **2036** and robots take the hands-on work around **2039**.
By forty I want a job where people want **a person** in the room.
do: Take the **electric vehicle** course and save a little more in year one.
Look at **teaching mechanics** at the college through a Saturday course.
Keep **testing** cars while he works out the next step.
feel: Quietly curious about **care work**, which he'd never said aloud.
S4.quote: People trust a mechanic and they trust a carer. It's the same thing: someone who turns up and fixes what's wrong.
fieldNote: Ten years opens up **two career ideas**: college teaching and care work.
His adaptability shows as **step by step** planning once a path is proven.
The **no savings** problem still limits any pay cut.

steps.text: Sign up for the Saturday teaching course at the college
Vote for the party promising paid apprenticeships in new trades
Keep doing MOT tests at the garage meanwhile

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The robots coming three years later sounds like a breather, but it's three years of customers with less money and Linda cutting hours. What would help is a retraining fund that pays your rent while you learn, and some guarantee a human still signs off safety tests for a while.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. Everyone asks about my job, but what matters is whether one of us can carry the other. With Theo's care job, for once, I think we'd manage, just about.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about my job, but what matters is whether one of us can carry the other.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old MOT tester** and workshop lead at a garage in a former mining town.
He and his boyfriend, a **care worker**, have about two weeks of bills saved.
He uses AI casually and would **learn the tools** to stay useful as they arrive.
In the faster AGI pictures he expects **cut hours** before job loss.
With **ten years**, he quietly considers teaching mechanics or moving into care.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the robot gap still means three years of customers with less money.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** that covers rent while you learn.
A rule that a **human signs off** safety tests for a while.
